options.text: p = F ÷ A
options.explanation: Force divided by the area it acts across.

options.text: p = F × A
options.explanation: Multiplying misstates the concentration.

options.text: p = A ÷ F
options.explanation: That inverts the relationship.

options.text: p = m ÷ V
options.explanation: That is density's equation.

questions.stem: A force spreads over a larger area. What happens to the pressure?

options.text: it doubles regardless
options.explanation: The change tracks the area ratio, not a fixed double.

options.text: it decreases, because the same force divides by more area
options.explanation: Larger denominators shrink the quotient.

options.text: it increases, because more area carries more force
options.explanation: The force is unchanged; only the spreading changes.

options.text: it stays the same
options.explanation: The area entered the equation; the answer changed.

questions.stem: What is the unit of pressure?

options.text: the joule
options.explanation: Joules measure energy.

options.text: the kilogram
options.explanation: Kilograms measure mass.

options.text: the pascal
options.explanation: One pascal is one newton per square metre.

options.text: the newton
options.explanation: Newtons measure force alone.

questions.stem: Which area counts in the pressure equation?

options.text: the object's total surface area
options.explanation: Only the pushed patch counts.

options.text: the floor's area beneath the whole room
options.explanation: The contact area, not the room's, enters.

options.text: the area of the force's arrow diagram
options.explanation: Diagrams carry no area for the equation.

options.text: the cross-sectional area the force acts across at right angles
options.explanation: Perpendicular contact is the definition.

questions.stem: A box rests on a table. The box is turned so it rests on its smallest face. The pressure it exerts

options.text: increases, because the same weight now squeezes a smaller area
options.explanation: Smaller contact patch, sharper pressure.

options.text: decreases, because the box is more stable
options.explanation: Stability is not the variable; area is.

options.text: stays the same, because the weight is unchanged
options.explanation: The weight is unchanged, but the division changed.

options.text: becomes zero, because the box is not moving
options.explanation: Static pushes still exert pressure.

questions.stem: State the pressure equation in symbols with each quantity's unit.
questions.modelAnswer: p = F ÷ A, where p is the pressure in pascals, F is the force in newtons and A is the cross-sectional area in metres squared.

questions.stem: State how pressure is defined in words.
questions.modelAnswer: Pressure is the concentration of a force — the force applied across each unit of area.

questions.stem: Explain why the area in the pressure equation must face the force at right angles.
questions.modelAnswer: The equation counts the push delivered onto a surface, and only the component perpendicular to that surface presses into it. The cross-sectional area is therefore the patch the force strikes head-on; a glancing contact would spread its effect along the surface instead.

questions.stem: A piston of cross-sectional area 0.02 m² carries a force of 900 N. Calculate the pressure it exerts.
Why does a drawing pin enter the surface rather than your thumb?

options.text: the push travels around the pin to avoid the thumb
options.explanation: Nothing travels around; the areas differ.

options.text: its sharp point concentrates the push into a small area, creating a large pressure there
options.explanation: The point is the pressure multiplier.

options.text: the pin is heavier than the surface
options.explanation: Weight is irrelevant to the direction.

options.text: the surface is softer than skin everywhere
options.explanation: The mechanism is area concentration, not softness alone.

questions.stem: What do a nail's pointed end and a tractor's wide tyres have in common?

options.text: both are designed to increase pressure
options.explanation: Tyres decrease it.

options.text: both rely on high friction
options.explanation: Friction is not the mechanism cited.

options.text: both engineer pressure through the contact area
options.explanation: One concentrates, the other spreads — same equation.

options.text: both reduce the force the machine applies
options.explanation: The forces are set by the hammer and the tractor's weight.

questions.stem: High heels press harder into soft ground than flat shoes because

options.text: heels apply a larger force
options.explanation: The wearer's weight — the force — is unchanged.

options.text: flat shoes weigh less
options.explanation: Shoe mass is not the driver.

options.text: the ground is softer for heels
options.explanation: The ground is the same ground.

options.text: the same weight acts across a smaller area
options.explanation: Smaller denominator, larger pressure.

questions.stem: A tractor is modified with narrower tyres. What happens on soft mud?

options.text: the pressure on the mud rises and the tractor sinks more easily
options.explanation: Narrower tyres shrink the contact area.

options.text: the pressure falls and the tractor floats
options.explanation: The change runs the other way.

options.text: nothing changes — mud ignores tyres
options.explanation: The mud feels the pressure difference.

options.text: the tractor's weight doubles
options.explanation: Weight is untouched by tyre choice.

questions.stem: Which design change would REDUCE the pressure of a footpath sign's base on a lawn?

options.text: balancing the sign on one corner
options.explanation: That shrinks the patch and raises pressure.

options.text: a wider base plate spreading the same weight
options.explanation: More area, less pressure per patch.

options.text: a sharper spike under the same weight
options.explanation: That raises the pressure.

options.text: a heavier sign
options.explanation: More force raises the pressure.

questions.stem: State why a nail's pointed end helps it enter a wall.
questions.modelAnswer: The point gives a very small contact area, so the hammer's force concentrates into a large pressure that drives the nail in.

questions.stem: State what a tractor's large tyres do to the machine's pressure on mud.
questions.modelAnswer: The large tyres spread the tractor's weight over a large area, reducing the pressure so it avoids sinking into the mud.

questions.stem: Explain why the drawing pin example involves the SAME force at both ends but different pressures.
questions.modelAnswer: The thumb's push transmits through the pin unchanged in size, but the two ends present different areas: the broad head against the thumb and the sharp point against the surface. Dividing the same force by different areas yields different pressures, which is why the pin bites the board and not the thumb.

questions.stem: An elephant's foot spans 0.1 m² and presses with 5000 N; a stiletto heel spans 0.0001 m² and presses with 500 N. Which applies the greater pressure, and by how many times?
questions.modelAnswer: Elephant: 5000 ÷ 0.1 = 50 000 Pa; heel: 500 ÷ 0.0001 = 5 000 000 Pa, so the heel applies 100 times the elephant's pressure.
